330.title: The good of all
330.hook: the year ends where every Ardas ends, asking good for everyone
330.howItsDone: Every Ardas, in every gurdwara and at home, ends with the line asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all, before the congregation calls out the jaikara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the depths: the Granth's themes, the Bhagats, history and grief, and your line, deep water, crossed. Today, the next to last day of the year, we end where every Ardas ends. Day three hundred thirty.

Amritsar, the 1700s, a spring morning at Vaisakhi. Riders come in from every direction: bands that spend the rest of the year scattered, sometimes quarreling, often hunted. For a few days they camp side by side, sit together before the Guru Granth Sahib, and decide things as one. That gathering had a name, which you met on day 289: the Sarbat Khalsa. Sarbat, everyone. Everyone who belonged. Every Ardas, to this day, ends with that same word. But in the prayer, it reaches a long way past the riders camped at Amritsar. Today: the good of all.
screen: `AMRITSAR, VAISAKHI, THE 1700S.` → `THE SARBAT KHALSA GATHERS.` → `THE SAME WORD, REACHING FURTHER.`

segments.voice: On day 251 we took the Ardas's last line apart: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Rising spirits through the Name, and, by your will, the good of all. Today, just one word from it, because you've now met that word twice. Sarbat. In the Sarbat Khalsa, it meant the whole Khalsa: every band, every leader, everyone who belonged, gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib. In the Ardas, the same word stretches past every border. Not the whole Khalsa. The whole of everything. Sarbat da bhala: the good of all, full stop. Now think about who says it. This year's path walked through a community hunted in the forests, massacred in 1746 and again in 1762, turned away from a harbor in 1914, attacked in its holiest place and in its own neighborhoods. The Ardas remembers much of that. And then it doesn't end with, protect our own, or, defeat our enemies. It ends by asking good for everyone, and Sikh teachers often say plainly that this includes the people who did the hurting. It grows out of what the Gurus taught: one light in every person; no enemy and no stranger, as Guru Arjan sings on Ang 1299. And notice tere bhane, by your will. The prayer doesn't tell God what everyone's good should look like. It asks, and leaves the shape of it to the Giver. That's a fitting place to stand at the end of a year: three hundred thirty days of stories, practices, the Japji and the depths, and a prayer whose last word reaches past the people saying it. For everyone, not just us.
screen: `SARBAT KHALSA: THE WHOLE KHALSA.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA: THE WHOLE OF EVERYTHING.` · `A HURT PEOPLE ASKS GOOD FOR ALL.` · `BY YOUR WILL, IN YOUR WAY.` · then, large: `FOR EVERYONE, NOT JUST US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish good for three people, chosen from this year. Settle, and breathe. First, someone who taught you something this year, in any way at all. Picture them, and wish them well, in your own words or none. Next, someone on the other side of a disagreement you're in, at home, at work, or in the news. Wish them well too, even a little. Last, someone far away whose story you heard on this path and will never meet. Wish them well. If you pray, you can hold all three in your prayer. If not, just hold them. The bell holds the time.
The good of all. Sarbat da bhala: the last words of every Ardas, asking good for everyone.
Your line: for everyone, not just us. Today, do one small good thing for someone outside your circle, someone who can't pay you back. Day three hundred thirty.

331.title: The big lookout
331.hook: year one is done; ahead lie the ranges: the daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru, the Granth itself
331.howItsDone: Sikhs understand themselves as lifelong learners of the Guru, and the Ardas that closes most gatherings ends by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, and the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the good of all: every Ardas ends by asking good for everyone, sarbat da bhala, and your line, for everyone, not just us. Today is the last day of year one. Day three hundred thirty-one.

You know the moment near the top of a long hike. Your legs are tired, so you stop and turn around, and there it is: the whole valley you walked through, small and golden below you. Then you turn the other way, and there are more mountains. Bigger ones, blue in the distance. Most people feel two things at once right there. I made it. And, look how much more there is. That's exactly where you're standing. Three hundred thirty-one days. Today: the big lookout.
screen: `A TIRED HIKER TURNS AROUND.` → `THE VALLEY BEHIND, SMALL AND GOLDEN.` → `MORE MOUNTAINS AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the word Sikh itself. It is usually traced to an old Indian word for a student, a disciple, a learner. Sikhs often put it simply: a Sikh is someone who keeps learning from the Guru. Not someone who finishes. So a year of learning doesn't end with a diploma. It ends at a lookout. Turn around first. You began with first words: seva, Waheguru, Ik Onkar, langar, sangat. Then the stories: ten Gurus, one light. Then the practices: kirtan, simran, Nitnem, a visit to the gurdwara. Then the Japji, pauri by pauri, all thirty-eight and the saloks. Then the depths: the Granth's great themes, Kabir and Farid, the rehat, the history, and the grief of 1984 carried carefully. That's the valley. Now turn and face the other way. Four ranges stand out there. First, the daily banis: Jaap Sahib tomorrow, then Anand Sahib, Rehras, Kirtan Sohila, Sukhmani, the prayers many Sikhs say morning and evening. Then the long story: Sikh history told slowly, century by century. Then the ways of the Guru: how Sikhs live it, day to day. And then the Granth itself, fourteen hundred thirty pages, the Guru Sikhs bow to. Daunting? Sikhs have a phrase for the spirit to meet it with, and you met it on day fifteen: chardi kala. Rising spirits. An unbeaten, upward-facing mind. It sits in the very last line of the Ardas, right beside the good of all from yesterday. Chardi kala isn't pretending things are easy. The Sikh story has plenty of hard days in it, and you walked through some of them. It's facing forward anyway, in good heart, because the road is long and the company is good. That's the lookout: grateful behind, awake ahead.
screen: `SIKH: A LEARNER WHO KEEPS LEARNING.` · `THE VALLEY: WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES, DEPTHS.` · `THE RANGES: BANIS, STORY, WAYS, GRANTH.` · `CHARDI KALA: FACE FORWARD, IN GOOD HEART.` · then, large: `WOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look out a window. Find one, any one, and let your eyes go as far as they can. A rooftop, a tree, a strip of sky. Breathe slowly. For the first part, think back over the year: one word, one story, one practice that stayed with you. Then let your gaze go farther, to the edge of what you can see, and just notice that there is more out there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru under your breath, the first word many Sikhs reach for in wonder. If you don't, simply let yourself be a little amazed. The bell holds the time.
The big lookout. The top of year one: the valley of words, stories, practices and depths behind you, and the ranges of the banis and the Granth ahead, met in chardi kala.
Your line: wow. Today, catch one moment that earns it, a sky, a kindness, a sentence that lands, and actually say it. Day three hundred thirty-one. Year one, done.

332.title: The Tenth Guru's morning praise
332.hook: Jaap Sahib is a rolling litany of the Timeless One's qualities, said each morning after Japji
332.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Jaap Sahib every morning as part of Nitnem, right after Japji Sahib, often from memory or a small prayer book (gutka), and it takes roughly fifteen to twenty minutes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the big lookout: the valley of year one behind you, the ranges ahead, and your line, wow. Today you take the first step into the first range, the daily banis. Year two begins. Day three hundred thirty-two.

What do people do when one sentence isn't enough? Listen to a best man at a wedding. He doesn't say, my friend is good. He says: loyal, ridiculous, the one who drove four hours at midnight, the one who still remembers your mother's birthday. Love turns into a list. The list speeds up. Everyone laughs, and somebody cries. Sikhs have a morning prayer built exactly like that, a list that keeps going, faster and faster, because no single word will do. It comes right after Japji. Today: the Tenth Guru's morning praise.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE ISN'T ENOUGH.` → `LOVE TURNS INTO A LIST.` → `THE LIST SPEEDS UP.`

segments.voice: Its name is Jaap Sahib. Jaap comes from jap, to repeat, to recite, the same root as japna, the steady repeating of the Name. Sahib is a word of respect, the way Sikhs honor a bani. So the title means something like: the honored recitation. Sikh tradition credits it to Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, who lived from 1666 to 1708. It isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. It opens a second collection, the Dasam Granth, the book linked with the tenth Guru. In the standard text it runs to one hundred ninety-nine stanzas. And almost all of it is one thing: names. Qualities of the Timeless One, line after line. Many of them begin with a small sound, a, which means without. Without form. Without birth. Without fear. Without end. It's a way of praising by saying: whatever you picture, it's more than that. The language is a rich mix. Mostly Braj, an old poetic Hindi, with words shaped like Sanskrit, and passages in Persian, full of Persian and Arabic words. And the meter keeps changing, around ten different chhands, some stately, some so quick the words drum. Now its place in the day. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, lists the morning banis: Japji first, Guru Nanak's quiet wisdom; then Jaap, the Tenth Guru's praise; then ten short verses called the Tav Prasad Savaiye. The first Guru and the tenth, side by side every morning. Japji thinks. Jaap sings, and keeps moving. For the next thirty days we'll walk through it, a few names at a time.
screen: `JAAP: TO REPEAT, TO RECITE.` · `THE TENTH GURU, 199 STANZAS.` · `A: WITHOUT FORM, WITHOUT BIRTH, WITHOUT END.` · `JAPJI FIRST, THEN JAAP.` · then, large: `PRAISE AT PACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to the first two minutes of Jaap Sahib. If you have a recording, play it now and let it run while you sit. You don't need to follow the words yet. Notice how the lines keep coming, how the pace pulls you along, how it never stops to explain itself. If you can't play anything, sit quietly and listen to whatever sounds are around you, one after another, without naming them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once at the end. The bell holds the time.
Jaap Sahib. The honored recitation: Guru Gobind Singh's long, quickening list of the Timeless One's qualities, said each morning right after Japji.
Your line: praise at pace. Today, when you admire something or someone, don't stop at one word. Find three, quickly, and say them. Day three hundred thirty-two.

333.title: No mark, no caste
333.hook: the opening stanza says He has no mark or sign, no color, caste or lineage (Jaap 1)
333.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this opening stanza every morning as the start of Jaap Sahib, and the Gurus' rejection of caste is lived out in langar, where all sit in one row, and in the shared Khalsa names Singh and Kaur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaap Sahib, the Tenth Guru's morning praise, and your line, praise at pace. Did you find three quick words for someone? Today, the very first stanza. Day three hundred thirty-three.

A conference badge. Name, company, job title, maybe a little colored dot for vegetarian. Within two seconds of meeting someone, you've read it, and they've read yours. Most of the world works this way. Accent, neighborhood, last name, the logo on a shirt: little marks that tell everyone where to put you. In seventeenth-century Punjab the marks were sharper still: caste, clan, the sign painted on a forehead, the cut of a robe. And the Tenth Guru opens his great praise by taking every one of those marks and saying: none of these apply. Today: no mark, no caste.
screen: `A BADGE: NAME, COMPANY, TITLE.` → `MARKS THAT TELL US WHERE TO PUT PEOPLE.` → `JAAP OPENS: NONE OF THESE APPLY.`

segments.voice: The first stanza of Jaap Sahib begins with a list of absences. Its opening words, chakr chihan ar baran jaat ar paat nahin jih, mean roughly: the One who has no mark and no sign, no color, no caste, no lineage. Look at that list. Chakr is a mark, the kind of sign some religious groups wore to show which god or sect they followed. Chihan is any sign at all. Baran is varna, the old word for the four great classes of Indian society, and it also means color. Jaat is caste. Paat is lineage, the family line. These were the labels that decided, in the Guru's world, who could eat with whom, marry whom, learn which texts, enter which temple. The stanza goes on: form, complexion, outline, dress, nobody can describe them. So before Jaap praises a single quality, it clears the table. Whatever badge you would pin on the Divine, take it off. Here's why that lands for Sikhs. The Gurus had been taking those same badges off people for two centuries. Langar, where everyone sits in one row and eats the same food. Sangat, where anyone may sit before the Guru. And in 1699, tradition says, the Tenth Guru gave the new Khalsa shared names, Singh and Kaur, so that a surname could no longer announce a caste. Many Sikhs hear the opening of Jaap and the founding of the Khalsa as one idea from two sides: the One has no caste, and so the people who bow to that One shouldn't wear caste either. No mark, no sign.
screen: `NO MARK, NO SIGN, NO COLOR, NO CASTE.` · `THE BADGES THAT SORTED PEOPLE.` · `CLEAR THE TABLE BEFORE THE PRAISE.` · `SINGH AND KAUR: SHARED NAMES.` · then, large: `NO MARK, NO SIGN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one label you use for yourself. Pick one: a job title, a school, a type you call yourself, the smart one, the difficult one, the busy one. Hold it in your mind for a breath. Then set it down, as if you were unpinning a badge and laying it on a table. Sit for a little while without it. Who is here when that word is gone? You don't have to answer. Just breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly. The bell holds the time.
No mark. The opening of Jaap Sahib: the One has no mark or sign, no color, caste or lineage, and no form anyone can describe.

Your line: no mark, no sign. Today, when you catch yourself sorting someone by a badge, an accent, a job, a neighborhood, take the badge off in your mind and look again. Day three hundred thirty-three.

334.title: King of kings
334.hook: He is called king of kings and lord of countless Indras (Jaap 1)
334.howItsDone: Sikhs bow their foreheads to the floor (matha tekna) before the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara, and often speak of the Guru as sachcha patshah, the true king.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no mark: the One with no sign, no caste, no lineage, and your line, no mark, no sign. Did you take a badge off someone in your mind? Today, the same stanza turns from what He isn't to what He rules. Day three hundred thirty-four.

Picture Delhi in the late 1600s. The emperor sits in a hall of white marble. His titles take a full breath to read aloud, and one of the oldest of them, from Persian, is shahanshah: king of kings. Courtiers bow to the floor. Coins carry his name. Far to the north, in the hills near Anandpur, a young Guru is writing a hymn. And in its very first stanza he takes that same title, king of kings, and gives it away. Not to any man on any throne. Today: king of kings.
screen: `DELHI, LATE 1600S: A MARBLE HALL.` → `SHAHANSHAH: KING OF KINGS.` → `A GURU GIVES THE TITLE AWAY.`

segments.voice: After the list of absences, the first stanza of Jaap turns. The One is achal moorat, an unmoving form; self-lit, of boundless power. Then comes a line with two great titles in it. Kot indr indraan: lord of millions of Indras. Saahu saahaan: king of kings. Start with Indra. In the old stories of India, Indra is the king of the gods, ruler of a shining heaven, the one who sends the rain. To call the One lord of a single Indra would already be enormous. Jaap says millions of them. Imagine every heaven anyone has ever pictured, each with its own crowned king, and the Timeless One above them all. Then saahu saahaan, the Persian title the emperors used. In one line the Guru gathers the highest ruler of the old Indian heavens and the highest ruler of the Persian-speaking courts, and sets both below the One. Why does that matter? Because a person who believes there is a King above every king stands differently in front of power. Sikhs call the Guru sachcha patshah, the true king, and they bow their heads to the Guru, to the Guru Granth Sahib, not to thrones. Sikh history is full of people who would not bow where their conscience said no, and who paid for it. The line isn't a protest slogan. It's praise. But praise like this changes posture. If the One is above every throne, then every throne on earth is borrowed. And the head you bow in the morning is a head that doesn't need to bow to fear.
screen: `ACHAL MOORAT: THE UNMOVING FORM.` · `LORD OF MILLIONS OF INDRAS.` · `SAAHU SAAHAAN: KING OF KINGS.` · `EVERY EARTHLY THRONE IS BORROWED.` · then, large: `ABOVE EVERY THRONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow your head for a moment. Sit comfortably. Let your chin drop slowly toward your chest, as if you were in a gurdwara, where Sikhs bow their foreheads before the Guru Granth Sahib. Stay there for a few breaths. Notice what a bow feels like from the inside: the neck softening, the eyes lowering, the mind getting quieter. Then lift your head slowly and sit tall. Bowed, then upright. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow. The bell holds the time.
King of kings. Saahu saahaan in the first stanza of Jaap: the One is lord of millions of Indras and above every emperor.
Your line: above every throne. Today, when someone's title or status makes you shrink a little, remember the line, straighten your back, and stay kind. Day three hundred thirty-four.

335.title: Named by deeds
335.hook: no one can tell all His names; the wise name Him by His works (Jaap 1)
335.howItsDone: Sikhs use many names for the Divine, Waheguru, Akal Purakh, Gobind, Kartar, and many of them, like Kartar (the Creator) and Dayal (the Merciful), are names drawn from what the One does.

segments.voice: Yesterday, king of kings, lord of millions of Indras, and your line, above every throne. Today, the last two lines of that same first stanza, and a question: if the One has no mark, what do you call Him? Day three hundred thirty-five.

Every apartment building has them. The neighbors whose names you never learned. So you name them by what they do. The guy who waters the plants at six. The woman who always holds the elevator. The kid practicing trumpet, badly, with total commitment. You don't know who they are on paper. You know them by their deeds. And honestly, that might be the truer name. The first stanza of Jaap Sahib ends on exactly this idea. Today: named by deeds.
screen: `NEIGHBORS WHOSE NAMES YOU NEVER LEARNED.` → `THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE ELEVATOR.` → `KNOWN BY WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: The first stanza of Jaap has stripped away every label: no mark, no caste, no form anyone can draw. It has called the One king of kings. Now it reaches its last two lines. First, the whole of creation speaks: gods, humans, demons, even the forests and the grass, and what they say is net net. Not this, not this. It's a very old phrase in Indian thought, used for a reality so large that every description has to be refused. Then the stanza asks the question it has been building to. Who can tell all Your names? Nobody. And then the answer: the wise speak Your karam naam. Karam means deeds, works, actions. Naam means name. Names drawn from what You do. That's the hinge of the whole hymn. Everything Jaap is about to say, salutation to the Merciful, salutation to the Protector, the Giver, the Destroyer of cruelty, these are deed-names. Not a passport. A list of what the One has been seen to do. Guru Arjan says something close in the Guru Granth Sahib, on page one thousand eighty-three: the tongue speaks names made from Your deeds, and Sat Naam, the true Name, is Your name from before all beginnings. So Sikhs hold two things together. There's a Name beyond all naming. And there are countless names that come from noticing: mercy here, protection there, a gift that arrived on time. The wise, Jaap says, don't argue about the first. They keep a record of the second.
screen: `NET NET: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` · `WHO CAN TELL ALL YOUR NAMES?` · `KARAM NAAM: NAMES FROM DEEDS.` · `ANG 1083: DEED-NAMES AND SAT NAAM.` · then, large: `NAMED BY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing you've seen the Divine do, or, if that language doesn't fit you, one thing life has done for you that you didn't arrange. A recovery. A stranger's help. A morning that came after a terrible night. Give it a deed-name, like Jaap does: the one who sent help, the one who kept me. Hold that name quietly and breathe with it. If you pray, you can say it with Waheguru. If you don't, just let it be a thank-you. The bell holds the time.
Named by deeds. Karam naam: no one can tell all the One's names, so the wise name Him by His works.
Your line: named by deeds. Today, give someone a deed-name out loud: thank you, the one who always remembers. Let them hear what you've noticed. Day three hundred thirty-five.

336.title: The snake's gait
336.hook: the next stanzas move in a meter named for a snake's gliding motion
336.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the bhujang prayat stanzas of Jaap Sahib in a steady, rolling rhythm, often quickly and from memory, and in a group the shared meter keeps everyone together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, named by deeds: no one can tell all His names, so the wise name Him by His works. That was the end of Jaap's first stanza. Today, the hymn changes its walk. Day three hundred thirty-six, the end of a week.

Have you ever watched a snake cross a path? It doesn't step. It doesn't hop. It pours. A small ripple starts at the head and travels down the whole body, and the snake is somewhere else before you've decided whether to be scared. No jerks, no pauses, one smooth wave after another. Indian poets heard that motion in certain rhythms of words, and they gave one meter a name for it. When Jaap Sahib leaves its first stanza, it starts to move exactly like that. Today: the snake's gait.
screen: `A SNAKE CROSSES THE PATH.` → `IT DOESN'T STEP. IT POURS.` → `A RHYTHM NAMED FOR THAT MOTION.`

segments.voice: The meter is called bhujang prayat. Bhujang is a snake. Prayat means going, moving. So, the snake's going, the snake's gait. It's an old meter of Sanskrit poetry, and Guru Gobind Singh uses it for long stretches of Jaap. Here's how it works. Each line is built from four little groups of three syllables, and every group goes the same way: short, long, long. Da, DUM, DUM. Listen to the opening of the second stanza: na-mas-tvam, a-kaa-le. Short, long, long. Short, long, long. Then the next line: na-mas-tvam, kri-paa-le. And the next: na-mas-tvam, a-roo-pe. Then: na-mas-tvam, a-noo-pe. Once you hear it, you can't stop hearing it. Each group is a small wave, and the waves keep rolling, line after line, the way a snake's body carries one ripple into the next. Why does the rhythm matter in a prayer? Because Jaap is meant to be said, out loud, often fast, often from memory, often by a whole room together. A steady meter is what lets hundreds of people glide through dozens of salutations without losing their place. The rhythm carries the words, so the mind is free to carry the meaning. And this is where the week ends. Seven days ago you were at the lookout. Since then you've met Jaap, the Tenth Guru's morning praise; the One with no mark and no caste; the king of kings above every throne; and the names drawn from deeds. Now the hymn begins to glide.
screen: `BHUJANG: SNAKE. PRAYAT: GOING.` · `SHORT, LONG, LONG, FOUR TIMES A LINE.` · `NAMASTVAM AKAALE, NAMASTVAM KRIPAALE.` · `THE RHYTHM CARRIES THE WORDS.` · then, large: `GLIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read four lines in rhythm. Say them slowly first, tapping your knee on each long syllable. Namastvam akaale. Namastvam kripaale. Namastvam aroope. Namastvam anoope. Short, long, long. Now say them once more, a little faster, and let them run together like one long wave. Don't worry about the meaning yet; that's the next few days. Then stop, and let your breath find its own smooth rhythm, in and out, no jerks, no pauses. The bell holds the time.
Bhujang prayat. The snake's gait: a meter of short, long, long, four times a line, that Jaap Sahib glides in for long stretches.
Your line: glide. Today, pick one ordinary task, walking, washing up, typing, and do it in a smooth, unhurried rhythm, no jerks. Day three hundred thirty-six. A week, done.
